Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette:
Kwame is a 68-year-old widowed Ghanaian-American man who works as a senior policy analyst for a federal health agency in Washington, D.C. He was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged hospitalisation eighteen months ago, during which he was placed in an intensive care unit for three weeks after a sudden cardiac arrest that left him clinically dead for several minutes before resuscitation. He had been preparing a briefing document at his desk when the event occurred - colleagues found him slumped in his chair, unresponsive - and the first responders who arrived described the scene to him later in terms he has never been able to forget. He has a PCL-5 score of 77, placing him in a range consistent with severe post-traumatic stress, and he presents to the current clinic having exhausted what he describes as his own private attempts to manage.

In the weeks following his discharge, Kwame returned to work earlier than his cardiologist advised, partly because the structure of the office felt safer than the silence of the home he had shared with his late wife. He told himself the worst was over. But the memory of the cardiac event did not behave as a past thing. It returned not as recollection but as re-occurrence - a sensation of the chest tightening, the sudden darkness, the absence of breath - and when it did, it felt to Kwame with full physiological conviction that it was happening right now rather than something that is over. These intrusive returns were not always overwhelming; sometimes he could recall the sequence of events with an almost clinical detachment, as though it had happened to a stranger, the emotional content drained entirely from the images. But at other times the memory arrived with such force that he had to stop whatever he was doing - mid-sentence in a briefing, mid-paragraph in a policy draft - simply to survive the wave of it.

The memory's unpredictability began to reshape how Kwame moved through his days. Because the intrusions carried such vivid physical immediacy, he had come to believe that his body could not be trusted to distinguish between danger and safety. Each time the memory returned with its full sensory weight, his nervous system responded as though the arrest were recurring, and this physiological response - the racing pulse, the muscular bracing, the inability to draw a full breath - confirmed for him that his body was still in danger even when no external threat existed. He was certain, in a way that felt empirical rather than fearful, that his body had become an unreliable instrument, prone to betrayal without warning. This belief kept him in a state of constant physical vigilance: his body felt perpetually tense and primed, and he remained on guard even inside his own apartment, scanning for the internal signal that would tell him something was wrong.

The appraisals themselves fed the threat system in a way that was difficult to interrupt. Because Kwame interpreted every somatic fluctuation - a missed heartbeat, a moment of breathlessness after climbing stairs - as evidence that his body was again failing him, the perceived threat never fully receded. This sustained sense of danger in turn made the traumatic memory more accessible, more easily triggered, and harder to contextualise as past. At his desk in the agency's open-plan office, the particular quality of fluorescent light and the ambient sound of keyboards had become potent retrieval cues - close enough to the sensory texture of that afternoon to pull the memory forward. The intrusions then reinforced his conviction that his body was operating outside his control, which deepened the threat appraisal, which kept his nervous system mobilised, which made the next intrusion more likely.

Over the past year, concentration has become genuinely impaired - he loses the thread of complex policy arguments mid-analysis, something that was never true of him before - and he has begun to fear that even his professional competence is eroding. What frightened him most, and what finally brought him to seek help, was the growing sense that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again - that the numbness he sometimes felt during recall was not a phase but a permanent condition, the emotional life he had shared with his wife now doubly inaccessible. He arrived at the first session quiet and precise, carrying a folder of his own notes. He hoped, he said, to understand what was happening inside him. He was not sure he believed it could be changed.
